glossary.Abscess: A walled-off collection of pus inside tissue.
glossary.Fistula: An abnormal tract connecting two epithelial surfaces, here the anal canal and the perianal skin.
glossary.Anal glands: Small glands opening into the anal crypts that secrete mucus into the anal canal.
glossary.Immunosuppression: Reduced immune function, from drugs such as steroids or from diseases such as HIV.
glossary.Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell.
glossary.External opening: The hole of a fistula on the skin near the anus, where discharge appears.
glossary.Internal opening: The hole of a fistula inside the anal canal, usually at the dentate line.
glossary.Perianal sepsis: Infection around the anus, such as an abscess, which can spread or become systemic.
glossary.Systemic infection: Infection affecting the whole body, causing fever, raised heart rate or sepsis.
glossary.Anal canal: The last 3 to 4 cm of the gut, from the rectum to the anal opening.
glossary.Perianal skin: The skin around the anal opening.
glossary.General Surgery: The surgical specialty covering the abdomen and bowel, including colorectal problems.
glossary.Colorectal: Relating to the colon, rectum and anus.
glossary.Sphincter: A ring of muscle that closes an opening; the anus has an internal and an external sphincter.
glossary.Levator ani: The sheet of pelvic floor muscle that supports the rectum and other pelvic organs.
glossary.Epithelium: The lining layer of cells covering a surface; once a tract is lined with it, it stays open.
glossary.Wound healing: The body's repair of damaged tissue, slowed by diabetes, steroids and poor blood supply.
glossary.Diabetes mellitus: A long-term condition of high blood glucose that weakens immunity and slows healing.
